messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Camila was twelve years old when her body turned against her. What started as a low fever became pediatric sepsis, and she spent three weeks in a pediatric intensive care unit where the silence between machine alarms felt more dangerous than the alarms themselves. She can still taste the bitter potassium chloride they gave her through her IV—a metallic, chemical film that coats her tongue whenever the memory surfaces. But she cannot hold the memory for long. Something in her shoves it away before the full picture arrives, and she has never been able to put what happened into words, not for a therapist, not for her mother, not even for herself.

Now twenty-two, working as an accountant for a mid-sized firm in Miami, Camila has made a quiet life inside spreadsheets and columns. Numbers are safe. They either add up or they don’t—no hidden danger. But the office itself is not safe. When the room goes still during tax season, everyone bent over their calculators, that same hospital silence presses in on her. Her chest tightens, her palms sweat, and she is certain something terrible is about to break. And when a client’s report takes longer than expected to arrive, her mind jumps immediately to the worst: the numbers are wrong, the audit will fail, she will lose her job. That physical jolt—the racing heart, the shallow breath—pulls the memory with it. She tastes the potassium again, feels the cold of the hospital bed, and the image flickers for a moment before she slams it shut.

But the damage is done. After these episodes, Camila withdraws. She stops talking to the coworker at the next desk because she is sure they cannot understand what she has been through. The isolation feels absolute. She used to be the kind of person who laughed easily, who brought pastries to the office on Fridays. Now she finds herself unable to remember what that felt like. Happiness is a foreign language. Every delay, every silence, every flash of taste proves to her that she is powerless. She cannot stop bad things from happening. She could not stop the sepsis when she was twelve, and she cannot stop the dread now.

Over the months, Camila has started arriving to work early so she can leave before the office becomes too quiet. She avoids the break room during slow afternoons. She has stopped checking her email after six in the evening because a delayed reply makes her spiral. Her manager has noticed, twice, that she requested to work from home on days when quarterly reports are due—waiting for numbers is unbearable. Camila knows this is not sustainable. She came to therapy last week because she spent an entire Tuesday sitting in her car in the parking lot, unable to go inside, the taste of potassium on her tongue, convinced that if she walked through the door something catastrophic would happen. She is afraid she will never be the happy person she was before. But she is also, underneath that, afraid to hope that she could become that person again.
